comments.body:
In the 'Multiplicative form' Remark (after Corollary cor:approx), it is claimed that computing $\Phi=n\log c_\sigma-L^\ast$ within 'a suitable constant multiplicative factor' is NP-hard, because 'on those instances $\mathrm{OPT}/(2\sigma^2)$ values for the two cases differ by a factor bounded away from 1'. This is FALSE in general.

The reduction's two cases are $\mathrm{OPT}(X,k)\le T$ vs. $\mathrm{OPT}(X,k)\ge T+1$. The ratio of the $\Phi$ values is therefore at most $\approx (T+1)/T$, which tends to $1$ as $T\to\infty$. Hence there is NO constant multiplicative gap unless $T$ is bounded, and the conclusion 'there is a constant approximation threshold below which the (normalized) problem is intractable' is not established. Moreover, on hard instances $\mathrm{OPT}$ can equal $0$ (data partition exactly into $k$ atoms), making $\Phi=E$ with $0\le E\le n\log k$, so the ratio comparison is meaningless.

Fix: either delete the multiplicative claim, or prove a genuine multiplicative-gap reduction. A standard route is amplification by point duplication/padding so that $\mathrm{OPT}$ (and hence $\Phi$, accounting for the $E\le n\log k$ slack) differs by a constant factor between YES/NO instances; alternatively reduce from a gap/APX-hard clustering variant.
